passages.title: Case File Zero: Before the First City
passages.text:
The Provenance Office keeps one promise.  Nothing gets filed as fact until the evidence proves it.  Old claims drift as time passes.  Conquerors rewrite the past to look better.  Rivals erase what came before them.  Forgers invent whole records from nothing.  A new field Recorder's first job is simple.  Open the oldest case in the whole record, and find where solid ground begins.

For most of human history, people moved with the seasons, living in small bands and hunting and gathering wild food.  No single place could feed a group for long, so nobody built anything meant to last.  Then, in a few river valleys, people learned a new trick.  They planted seeds on purpose and waited for a harvest.  Farming grew more food than hunting ever had, and extra food let some people stop searching for their next meal.  They settled down instead, and villages grew into towns.  Some towns grew large enough to become the first cities.

Two rivers explain why the first cities rose where they did.  In Mesopotamia, the Tigris and the Euphrates flooded every year, spreading fresh soil across the land nearby.  That soil grew far more food than dry ground could.  The floods were hard to predict, though, coming early some years and late in others.  Managing that water took real teamwork, canals, walls, and shared rules.  Farther west, the Nile flooded on a far steadier yearly schedule, so Egyptian farmers could plan around it.  Deserts on both sides of the Nile kept most invaders away, and a steadier, safer valley let Egypt unite sooner.

Both rivers prove the same rule the Office repeats to every new Recorder.  Geography decided where a civilization could begin.  What people built next is where the record gets interesting.

passages.title: Recovered Entry: The Code of Hammurabi
passages.text:
This entry gathers the Provenance Office's own working translation.  It covers several clauses from the law code of Hammurabi.  Hammurabi was a king of Babylon in ancient Mesopotamia.  The stone the code was carved on still exists.  Nothing here is a forgery.  The dispute is not whether the code is real.  The dispute is what the code actually did for the people living under it.

The code's own opening lines state its purpose plainly.  Its laws exist so that a strong man cannot crush a weak one.  They exist so that a widow or an orphan can get a fair hearing.  Read alone, that sounds like protection for the whole kingdom equally.

The clauses that follow tell a more complicated story.  One clause covers a man of high standing who destroys another man's eye.  If the victim holds the same high standing, the attacker's own eye is destroyed in return.  A second clause covers that very same injury done to a man of common standing.  It orders a payment of silver instead of a matching injury.  A third clause covers that same injury done to an enslaved person.  It sets the payment lower still, at half the enslaved person's own value, paid to that person's owner.  The punishment changes with the victim's standing.  The injury itself never changes at all.

Other surviving clauses cover house builders, merchants, and farmers.  Most of them share this same pattern.  A careless builder whose work kills a house owner is put to death.  That same builder's careless work, if it only kills the owner's enslaved worker, costs him a replacement instead.

The Provenance Office files this entry as verified but unresolved.  The code's opening promise and its actual clauses do not fully agree.  Did Hammurabi mean to protect ordinary people?  Or did he mainly mean to keep each rank of society fixed in its place?  That is the real question every Recorder assigned to this case has to weigh.

passages.title: Case File: Two Kingdoms of the Nile
passages.text:
Egyptians believed their king, the pharaoh, was not an ordinary ruler.  They believed he held a kind of divine power.  His main job was keeping the whole world in balance, a balance Egyptians called ma'at.  Two pharaohs left a large mark on the record.  Hatshepsut ruled Egypt in her own right as a full pharaoh, not merely as a king's wife.  She sent a famous trading trip south along the coast.  Years later, Ramses the Second reigned for decades and built huge monuments.  He later signed one of the oldest peace deals in the whole record.

Religion shaped how Egyptians treated their own dead.  Egyptians believed a spirit needed a preserved body to survive into the next life, so skilled workers made mummies to stop a body from decaying.  Wealthier Egyptians built large tombs and filled them with goods the dead were thought to need on the trip ahead.  That belief is the real reason the pyramids exist at all.

South of Egypt, along the same river, sat the kingdom of Kush.  Egypt and Kush traded gold, ivory, and other goods for centuries, but their bond was never simply friendly.  Egypt's own armies took over Kush during Egypt's strongest era.  Years later, that balance flipped.  Kushite kings conquered Egypt itself and ruled it as pharaohs in their own right, keeping many Egyptian customs alongside their own.

The two peoples even wrote their history in different ways.  Mesopotamian scribes pressed wedge-shaped cuneiform marks into wet clay, using a cut reed, one tablet at a time.  Egyptian scribes instead drew or carved hieroglyphs onto papyrus and stone, a system built from hundreds of small pictures.  Both systems did the same basic job.  They let a record live on long after its maker was gone.

passages.title: Case File: A Covenant Without a Kingdom Yet
passages.text:
Most peoples in the old Near East worshipped many gods at once.  The Hebrew Bible describes something different taking root among a group later known as the Israelites.  It describes Abraham as the first to promise loyalty to one God alone.  In exchange, that account describes a covenant, a solemn promise of land and heirs.  That one choice is the seed of monotheism, the belief in exactly one God.  This whole file keeps coming back to that belief.

The Hebrew Bible next tells of years spent in Egypt.  Abraham's heirs became slaves there, under an Egyptian king.  It tells of Moses leading them out of that slavery.  That event is remembered as the Exodus.  At Mount Sinai, tradition holds that Moses got a code of law for his people to live by.  It renewed the same covenant Abraham had made years before.

After reaching the land of Canaan, judges first led the Israelites, called on only when trouble struck.  Later, the Israelites chose kings instead.  Saul became the first.  David, the second, united the tribes more firmly and made Jerusalem his capital.  David's son Solomon built the First Temple there, one central place for the tradition's most sacred rites.

For years after Solomon, three things stood as one.  A king ruled.  A Temple centered worship.  A covenant explained why both stood at all.  The Office's next entry tests exactly how strong that link really was.  Outside armies later tore two of those three things away.

passages.title: Case File: The Shortest File Outlasts Its Own Temple
passages.text:
This case file is the shortest one in the whole Office archive.  That is exactly what makes it worth checking closely.  A tradition without a king, a Temple, or a homeland of its own should have simply faded away.  It should have faded into the peoples around it.  The record shows it did not.

The first blow came when the Babylonian army conquered the kingdom of Judah.  The army destroyed the First Temple in Jerusalem and forced many Israelites into exile, far from their own land.  That exile is remembered as the diaspora.  It grew as more people scattered even further from home over later years.  Years later, Persian rulers let the exiles return and build a Second Temple on that same site.

The Second Temple stood for centuries.  Then a Roman army destroyed it too, during a revolt long after Israel's old kings had reigned.  This second loss should have finished the tradition for good.  Rome had already crushed the state.  Now the Temple, the tradition's central home, was gone too.

The record credits a teacher named Yohanan ben Zakkai with the turn that followed.  Tradition holds that he escaped the besieged city.  He got permission from Roman rulers to open a small school in a town called Yavneh.  Teaching there, without any Temple at all, he changed the tradition's whole center of gravity.  Priests had once made offerings in one sacred building.  Now study, prayer, and law took that place, and any group could carry those things with it, anywhere.

That shift is the real claim behind this file's short length, now fully checked.  The tradition outlived its own state and its own Temple.  It did not rebuild either one.  It proved instead that it had never truly leaned on them alone.

passages.title: Source A: The Athenian Account, Filed by the Aegean Desk
passages.text:
Greece's own land decided its shape long before any war began.  Mountains cut the land into small, separate pockets, and the sea reached almost every one of them.  No single valley could feed a kingdom big enough to rule the whole region.  Instead, dozens of separate city-states grew up.  Each one ran its own government.  Each one guarded its own coast.

Athens took its own government further than most cities dared.  Its assembly let adult male citizens vote directly on the city's laws.  This system is remembered as democracy, rule by the people themselves.  Enslaved people, foreigners, and women could not vote.  The system's real reach was smaller than the word alone suggests.  Still, within that limited group, Athens gave plain citizens a truly direct voice.  A culture built on open debate grew up alongside it.  A thinker named Socrates walked the city asking sharp questions.  His questions made easy ideas fall apart in public.

The Persian Empire invaded Greece twice.  Athens filed its own account of what really won the war.  Athenian soldiers stood almost alone at Marathon.  They turned back the first Persian invasion outright.  Years later, an even bigger force arrived.  Athens poured newly found silver into a huge navy.  The leader Themistocles pushed hard for this plan.  At Salamis, that navy trapped the Persian fleet in a narrow strait.  It wrecked the fleet outright.  The invasion's push broke for good.  The Persian king pulled back with most of his army.

This account does not deny that other cities fought bravely too.  It simply argues that ships, not soldiers, won the war.  A closing note from the Aegean Desk adds one more point.  Greek ways did not stay locked inside these city-states forever.  A Macedonian king named Alexander later carried them across a much wider empire.

passages.title: Source B: The Spartan-Leaning Account, Filed by the Peloponnese Desk
passages.text:
Sparta's own account of the Persian Wars starts with its government.  That government looked nothing like Athens.  Two kings ruled Sparta at once, checking each other's power.  A council of elders helped run the city.  A small board of overseers, called ephors, ran its daily business.  Plain citizens still met in an assembly.  Real power sat with a much smaller, older group than Athens ever let near its own choices.

Spartan life itself was built around one goal.  Every Spartan boy entered a harsh army training system at a young age.  He stayed a soldier his whole adult life.  A large group of unfree workers, called helots, farmed the land instead.  This let Spartan citizens stay in training at all times.  Sparta's government existed to keep that one army ready.  This account argues that readiness is exactly what saved Greece when Persia invaded.

The second Persian invasion arrived, and this file credits Sparta with the war's real turning points.  King Leonidas led a small, Spartan-led force.  His force held a narrow mountain pass at Thermopylae.  The Persian army there was many times its size.  The stand ended in defeat, but it bought Greece precious time.  It became a lasting sign of resistance.  The next year, an allied Greek army met the last Persian force on open ground at Plataea.  A Spartan leader led that army.  It beat the Persians outright.  The invasion was finally driven out of Greece for good.

This account treats the earlier sea battle at Salamis in a different way.  It calls Salamis one useful step among several, not the single moment that decided everything.  Two files, filed by two different desks, tell of the very same war.  The Office keeps both.  It refuses to force one account to lose.

passages.title: Case File: The Quiet Record of the Indus
passages.text:
Some files in the Office archive are quiet for a reason.  Nothing bad happened; the people involved simply cannot speak for themselves yet.  The Indus Valley civilization built some of the best-planned cities anywhere in the old world.  Mohenjo-daro and Harappa sat on careful grids.  Baked-brick homes linked to covered drains, an advanced setup for its time.

The Indus people also left behind a written script.  It was cut into thousands of small stone seals.  No scholar has ever managed to read it.  Every other early society in this record can be read straight, in its own words.  Court records, temple writings, and trader letters survive elsewhere.  The Indus people left none of that.  Whatever its people believed, ruled, or argued about stays locked behind an unread script.  This file treats that gap honestly instead of guessing past it.

Its fall is easier to weigh, though still not fully settled.  The clearest evidence involves shifting rivers.  One major stream that once fed Indus farms seems to have dried up or changed path.  Evidence also points to a weaker monsoon.  That means longer, harsher dry spells across the region.  Farming likely grew far harder to keep up.  Many of the biggest cities emptied out slowly, not all at once.  Scholars still argue over how much of the fall came from nature alone.

Sometime after the Indus cities faded, new migrants arrived from the northwest.  Many scholars think these Indo-Aryan migrants brought an early form of Sanskrit with them.  They brought a new set of faith practices too.  Those practices were set down in hymns called the Vedas.  The Vedas became the base the next file builds right on top of.

passages.title: Case File: Dharma, the Buddha, and an Emperor's Change of Heart
passages.text:
Many scholars think Vedic hymns arrived with the Indo-Aryan migrants.  Over time, they grew into a much larger faith, the one now known as Hinduism.  Hindus came to believe in dharma, a person's proper duty in life.  They also came to believe in karma, the belief that every act carries results that follow a person forward.  Vedic life also split into four broad groups, called varnas.  Birth decided which varna a person belonged to.  This setup shaped daily life for years afterward.

Years into this faith, a prince named Siddhartha Gautama gave up his easy life.  He had seen how much plain suffering filled the world.  He taught that suffering grows from craving, wanting things to be other than they are.  He taught that a strict path could end that craving for good.  His followers called him the Buddha, meaning the awakened one.  His teaching grew into a path open to anyone, no matter which varna a person had been born into.

Years later, an emperor named Ashoka ruled the Maurya Empire.  By then, it was the biggest state the Indian subcontinent had ever seen.  Early in his reign, Ashoka waged a brutal war against the kingdom of Kalinga.  His own carved words tell of a huge number of dead and captured.  They tell of his own horror at what the war had cost.  After Kalinga, Ashoka took up Buddhist ways.  He turned his huge state toward a strikingly new goal.  He had edicts cut into pillars and rock faces across his empire, pushing nonviolence, tolerance of other faiths, and the good of plain people, not more war.

Few rulers in the old record changed course that plainly.  Fewer still left the proof cut in stone for a Recorder to find, more than two thousand years later.

passages.title: Case File: Two Schools of Thought, One Unifying Emperor
passages.text:
The Huang He, known in English as the Yellow River, flooded often and hard.  Later writers gave it the name China's Sorrow.  Its floodwaters also carried rich soil that made the river valley worth the risk.  Early Chinese life grew up right along its banks.

China's earliest well-known dynasty was the Shang, which gave way to the Zhou dynasty.  The Zhou brought in an idea called the Mandate of Heaven.  Heaven gave a ruler the right to rule only while that ruler ruled fairly.  Heaven could pull that right back from a ruler who did not.  Zhou power weakened over the years.  China broke apart into rival states that fought nearly nonstop, in a time later called the Warring States era.

Two very different schools of thought tried to answer that long disorder.  Confucius taught that harmony grows from everyone filling their role well.  A ruler should act fairly, a child should honor a parent, and a friend should treat a friend with respect.  Order, in his teaching, comes from virtue lived by everyone at once.  A different path is tied to a teacher known as Laozi.  His teaching pointed closer to the other side.  It held that people should follow the Dao, the natural way of the world, without forcing events against their own natural course.

Neither school ended the fighting.  A ruler named Ying Zheng did.  He beat every rival state and named himself Qin Shi Huangdi, China's first emperor.  He set one standard for the empire's writing, money, and weights.  One system replaced the many different ones lands had used before.  He also moved right against ideas that threatened his new power.  Records written later say he ordered rival texts burned, with Confucian works a main target.  A number of scholars who defied the order were put to death too.  This is the record this file's own title borrows its warning from.

passages.title: Case File: The Han Restoration and the Long Road West
passages.text:
The Qin dynasty fell apart only a few years after its first emperor died.  Harsh rule and open revolt wore it down fast.  The Han dynasty that came next ruled far longer.  It made a choice the Qin never had.  Han rulers stopped treating Confucian teaching as a threat and put it back at the very center of government instead.

Han officials had to study the Confucian classics, the same texts the Qin had once tried to burn.  A person's grasp of those texts more and more shaped who could serve the state.  That change built a government of trained scholar-officials.  Birth alone no longer decided who ran the country, a lasting shift in how China chose its leaders.

Han China also reached much farther than its own borders.  A long web of trade routes linked Han cities to Central Asia and beyond.  Later writers called this web the Silk Road.  Caravans carried Chinese silk west and brought back horses, glass, and goods from far regions in return.  A Han official named Zhang Qian is often credited with opening these links.  He traveled west on a state trip, though trade along parts of the route likely came before his trip.  Goods were never the only thing moving along that road.  Ideas and faiths traveled with the traders who carried them.

Buddhism reached China this way, coming slowly from India along the same routes the silk traders used.  Buddhism took root beside Confucianism and Daoism rather than replacing either one.  Chinese thought, from that point on, kept following the very same road.

passages.title: Case File: Closing the File on Rome
passages.text:
This is the last entry in the whole case file.  It closes in a different way than every entry before it.  Rome does not open a new puzzle.  It answers back into every puzzle this file has already opened.

Rome began as a kingdom, then threw out its own king and became a republic instead.  Two elected consuls led it, along with a council called the Senate.  For years afterward, rich patrician families held nearly all the real power.  Plain plebeian citizens fought for a bigger share of it.  That fight in time produced the Twelve Tables, Rome's first written law code.  The code was posted in public so that every citizen, patrician or plebeian, could actually see the same laws applied to all, even though rank still shaped much of Roman life.  Compare that to Hammurabi's own code, filed at the very start of this record.  Its finished laws still punished the same crime in different ways, depending on who the victim was.

Rome's spot on a sea-facing peninsula pushed it steadily outward.  Rome fought the rival city of Carthage across three long wars and won.  Rome then held most of the Mediterranean coast.  A road web linked it all, moving troops and officials fast across huge distances.

The republic itself could not survive its own success.  A general named Julius Caesar seized power by force.  Senators feared he wished to rule as a king, and they killed him.  More years of civil war came next.  His adopted heir, Octavian, rose as Rome's first emperor, taking the name Augustus.  A republic without a king had lasted nearly five hundred years before an empire took its place.

Rome gave out citizenship widely across its conquered lands, a reach that went far past Athens and its own narrow assembly.  Athens had let its citizens vote right on the city's own laws, years earlier.  Rome also matched many of its own gods to Greek ones, simply giving them Roman names.  Rome took in Greek philosophy too.  The file that opened with a river and a code of law now closes with an empire, one built from nearly every civilization this record has ever checked.

partA.stem: According to the briefing, why did Egypt unite into a civilization sooner than the pattern in Mesopotamia?
choices: The Nile flooded on a far steadier yearly schedule, and deserts on both sides kept most invaders away.
The Tigris and the Euphrates flooded every year, spreading fresh soil across the land nearby.
Managing floodwater in Mesopotamia took real teamwork, canals, walls, and shared rules.
Farming grew more food than hunting ever had, so people could settle down.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: The floods were hard to predict, though, coming early some years and late in others.
Farming grew more food than hunting ever had, and extra food let some people stop searching for their next meal.
Deserts on both sides of the Nile kept most invaders away, and a steadier, safer valley let Egypt unite sooner.
Managing that water took real teamwork, canals, walls, and shared rules.

distractorRationale.1: This is true of Mesopotamia's rivers, but the passage credits Egypt's unity to the Nile's steadier schedule and the deserts, not to Mesopotamia's flooding.
distractorRationale.2: This describes the extra teamwork Mesopotamia's unpredictable floods required, the opposite of why Egypt needed less of that kind of organizing.
distractorRationale.3: This explains why farming let people settle down at all, a step every river-valley civilization shared, not the specific reason Egypt united sooner than Mesopotamia.

items.explain: The passage states directly that a steadier river and safer valley, thanks to protective deserts, let Egypt unite sooner than the flood-prone, harder-to-predict pattern in Mesopotamia.  The other choices each describe a true detail about rivers or farming that does not answer why Egypt specifically united faster.

items.stem: According to the case file, what does ma'at mean to Egyptians?
choices: The balance across the whole world that Egyptians believed the pharaoh's divine power was meant to keep.
The written record Mesopotamian scribes pressed into wet clay using a cut reed.
The peace deal Ramses the Second signed after reigning for decades.
The name of the trading trip Hatshepsut sent south along the coast.

distractorRationale.1: That describes cuneiform, Mesopotamia's writing system, a completely different topic from ma'at, the balance Egyptians believed their pharaoh's power was meant to keep.
distractorRationale.2: That peace deal is a specific achievement credited to Ramses the Second, not the word ma'at, which names a broader belief about balance tied to kingship itself.
distractorRationale.3: Hatshepsut's trading trip is a specific achievement of her own reign, not the word ma'at, which names the world-balance Egyptians believed every pharaoh's power was meant to keep.

items.explain: The case file states directly that Egyptians believed their pharaoh's main job was keeping the whole world in balance, a balance they called ma'at, tied to his divine power.  Each wrong choice names a real but separate detail, a writing system or a specific ruler's achievement, rather than the balance the word ma'at itself names.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that state the code's own opening promise of fair, equal protection.
spans: Its laws exist so that a strong man cannot crush a weak one.
They exist so that a widow or an orphan can get a fair hearing.
If the victim holds the same high standing, the attacker's own eye is destroyed in return.
A careless builder whose work kills a house owner is put to death.
The punishment changes with the victim's standing.
items.explain: The code's opening lines promise fair treatment for everyone, protecting a weak man from a strong one and giving a widow or an orphan a fair hearing.  The other three sentences describe what the actual clauses do once a real case is decided, which is exactly the gap this entry is filed to weigh.

items.stem: Choose the three details that are true, according to the case file on Egypt and Kush.
choices: Egyptians believed the pharaoh held a kind of divine power.
Mesopotamian scribes carved hieroglyphs onto papyrus and stone.
Egypt's own armies took over Kush during Egypt's strongest era.
Egypt and Kush never traded goods with each other.
Kushite kings later conquered Egypt and ruled it as pharaohs.

distractorRationale.1: The passage says Egyptian scribes carved hieroglyphs onto papyrus and stone, while Mesopotamian scribes pressed cuneiform into wet clay instead; this choice swaps which people used which system.
distractorRationale.3: The passage says Egypt and Kush traded gold, ivory, and other goods for centuries; it never says they had no trade at all.

items.explain: All three correct details come straight from the case file: the pharaoh's believed divine power, Egypt's early control over Kush, and Kush's later conquest of Egypt.  The two wrong choices each invert a real detail, swapping which civilization used which writing system or denying a trade relationship the passage actually describes.

Whether the stone the code was carved on is a forgery.
Whether Hammurabi actually ruled Babylon in ancient Mesopotamia.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?

The dispute is what the code actually did for the people living under it.

Swapping which region caused which outcome is exactly the confusion this table is built to catch.

partA.stem: According to the recovered entry, what actually happened when a man destroyed the eye of a person of common standing?
choices: The attacker paid a sum of silver instead of losing his own eye in return.
The attacker's own eye was destroyed in return, exactly as for a victim of high standing.
The attacker paid half the payment required for harming an enslaved person.
The attacker was put to death, the same punishment used for a careless builder.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: If the victim holds the same high standing, the attacker's own eye is destroyed in return.
It sets the payment lower still, at half the enslaved person's own value, paid to that person's owner.
It orders a payment of silver instead of a matching injury.
A careless builder whose work kills a house owner is put to death.

distractorRationale.1: That punishment, an eye for an eye, is what the clause sets for a victim of high standing, not common standing, according to the very next sentence in the entry.
distractorRationale.2: That sentence describes the payment set for an injury done to an enslaved person, half that person's own value paid to the owner, a different price entirely from the silver payment set for a victim of common standing.
distractorRationale.3: Death is the punishment the entry gives for a careless builder whose work kills a house owner, a completely different clause about builders, not the eye-injury clause.

items.explain: Closing the file, Rome is shown matching many of its own gods to Greek ones, simply giving them Roman names, and taking in Greek philosophy too, both direct callbacks to the civilization studied in an earlier case file.  The other sentences describe the wars against Carthage, Rome's road network, or its own civil war, none of which is an idea absorbed from an earlier civilization.

items.stem: Choose the three details that are true, according to the case file closing on Rome.
choices: Rome lost all three of its long wars against Carthage.
Rome overthrew its own king and became a republic before later becoming an empire.
Rome matched many of its own gods to Greek ones, simply giving them Roman names.
Rome's location on a sea-facing peninsula pushed it steadily outward.
Rome kept citizenship limited to the city of Rome itself and never extended it.

distractorRationale.0: The passage says Rome fought Carthage across three long wars and won, not that Rome lost all three.
distractorRationale.4: The passage says Rome gave out citizenship widely across its conquered lands, a reach far past a narrow assembly limited to one city.

items.explain: The three correct details trace the closing file's own account: Rome's shift from kingdom to republic to empire, its matching of many of its own gods to Greek ones under new Roman names, and the peninsula geography that pushed its expansion outward.  The two wrong choices each invert what the passage actually says about the Punic Wars and about how widely Rome extended citizenship.

partA.stem: According to the case file, what ended Rome's nearly five-hundred-year-old republic?
choices: Julius Caesar's seizure of power, his assassination, and the civil war that followed, ending with his heir Octavian becoming emperor as Augustus.
A foreign invasion that conquered Rome and installed a new king from outside.
The Senate voluntarily handed power to Carthage after losing the wars against it.
Patrician and plebeian families united peacefully and voted to create an empire.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Rome fought the rival city of Carthage across three long wars and won.
His adopted heir, Octavian, rose as Rome's first emperor, taking the name Augustus.
Senators feared he wished to rule as a king, and they killed him.
A general named Julius Caesar seized power by force.

distractorRationale.1: Julius Caesar, the general who seized power, was Roman himself, not a foreign king; the passage never describes any outside invasion.
distractorRationale.2: The passage says Rome fought Carthage across three wars and won; Rome defeated Carthage, it did not hand power to it.
distractorRationale.3: The transition was violent, not peaceful: senators killed Caesar out of fear he wanted to be king, and years of civil war followed before Augustus became emperor.

items.explain: The passage traces the republic's end directly: Julius Caesar seized power by force, senators killed him fearing he wanted to rule as a king, and after more years of civil war his heir Octavian became Rome's first emperor, taking the name Augustus.  The other choices each invent a peaceful, foreign, or unrelated cause the passage does not describe.

items.stem: In eight words or fewer, name what the closing file says Rome did with citizenship that Athens never did.
accept: gave it out widely across conquered lands
extended it far past a narrow assembly
spread citizenship widely across its conquered lands
gave citizenship to conquered peoples, not just one city
extended citizenship past one city's own assembly
spread it past one city to conquered lands
items.explain: The closing file draws the comparison directly: Rome gave out citizenship widely across its conquered lands, a reach that went far past Athens and its own narrow assembly, which let only adult male citizens of one city vote on its laws.  Any short phrasing naming that wider, conquered-lands reach, instead of Athens's narrower one-city model, earns credit here.

items.explain: Closing the file, the Recorder confirms the shortest file's own sequence one more time: the entry names Saul as the Israelites' very first king, before David united the tribes more firmly and Solomon later built the First Temple.  Each wrong choice names a real figure from the same entry, but one who ruled later or belongs to an earlier part of the story.

items.stem: For years afterward, rich {{0}} families held nearly all the real power.

choices: patrician
plebeian
consul

distractorRationale.1: Plebeian names the plain citizens who fought for a bigger share of power, the opposite rank from the wealthy families this sentence says already held nearly all of it.
distractorRationale.2: A consul was one of Rome's two elected leaders, an office held by one person, not the name for a whole wealthy family class.

items.quote: For years afterward, rich patrician families held nearly all the real power.
items.explain: The file names patrician families directly as the wealthy class that held nearly all of Rome's real power in the early republic.  Plebeian names the opposite, plainer class that fought for a share of that power, and consul names an elected office, not a whole family class, so neither term fits here.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that trace how the plebeians' fight for power actually led to Rome's first written law code.
spans: Plain plebeian citizens fought for a bigger share of it.
That fight in time produced the Twelve Tables, Rome's first written law code.
Rome began as a kingdom, then threw out its own king and became a republic instead.
Two elected consuls led it, along with a council called the Senate.
Compare that to Hammurabi's own code, filed at the very start of this record.
items.explain: The plebeians' own fight for a bigger share of power is named directly, and the file traces that fight straight to a result, the Twelve Tables, Rome's first written law code.  The other sentences describe Rome's founding as a republic, its consuls and Senate, or a later comparison, none of which is the fight-to-result chain itself.

partA.stem: The Recorder checks the Aegean Desk's own account one more time before closing the file.  According to that account, how far did Athenian democracy's real reach actually extend?
choices: It reached only adult male citizens directly, since enslaved people, foreigners, and women could not vote at all.
It reached every person living in Athens, with no exceptions at all.
It reached across every Greek city-state equally, uniting them under one shared vote.
It reached only Sparta's small council of elders and overseers.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Each one ran its own government.
Its assembly let adult male citizens vote directly on the city's laws.
Instead, dozens of separate city-states grew up.
Enslaved people, foreigners, and women could not vote.

distractorRationale.1: The assembly did let adult male citizens vote directly, but the very same account immediately adds that enslaved people, foreigners, and women could not vote at all, so it was never every person with no exceptions.
distractorRationale.2: This source says the opposite: dozens of separate city-states grew up, each running its own government, not one shared vote across all of Greece.
distractorRationale.3: This source describes Athens running its own government, separate from every other city-state; it never describes Sparta's council, which belongs to the other, Spartan-leaning account.

items.explain: The Aegean Desk's own account narrows its claim directly: the assembly let adult male citizens vote, then immediately states that enslaved people, foreigners, and women could not vote at all, meaning democracy's real reach stopped well short of everyone in Athens.  The other choices each widen or misplace that reach in a way this specific account never claims.

items.stem: While closing the file, the Recorder checks an earlier entry on Han China one more time.  According to that entry, who is often credited with opening the Silk Road's western links?
choices: Qin Shi Huangdi, the emperor who first unified China's writing, money, and weights.
Zhang Qian, a Han official who traveled west on a state trip.
Confucius, the philosopher whose teaching the Han later placed back at the center of government.
Yohanan ben Zakkai, the teacher who opened a school after a Temple's destruction.

distractorRationale.0: The entry credits Qin Shi Huangdi with unifying China under the earlier Qin dynasty, not with opening the Silk Road's western links, a Han-era achievement credited to Zhang Qian instead.
distractorRationale.2: The entry credits Confucius with a school of thought about harmony and proper roles, not with any trade route; opening the Silk Road's links is credited to the official Zhang Qian.
distractorRationale.3: Yohanan ben Zakkai belongs to an entirely different case file, on the Ancient Hebrews; the Han entry credits Zhang Qian, not him, with opening the Silk Road's western links.

items.explain: The Han entry credits a Han official named Zhang Qian with opening the Silk Road's western links, traveling west on a state trip even though trade along parts of the route likely came before him.  Each wrong choice borrows a name from a different ruler, philosopher, or even a different case file entirely, none of whom the entry connects to opening the route.
